subject: community-medicine
title: Aedes Surveillance: Larval Indices and Arboviral Transmission

steps.title: Aedes larval surveillance principles
steps.tx: To anticipate dengue and chikungunya epidemics, vector control squads conduct structured **entomological surveillance** targeting immature aquatic stages of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Technicians systematically inspect indoor and peri-domestic water collections, including unsealed plastic overhead tanks, earthenware storage pots, discarded automobile tyres, air coolers and flower pots, sampling water to enumerate larvae and compute standardized community transmission indices.
steps.say: Entomological teams inspect homes and yards for stagnant water in storage pots, air coolers and discarded tyres, collecting larvae to calculate transmission risk indices.

steps.title: Breteau index: containers per hundred houses
steps.tx: Among entomological indicators, the **Breteau index** provides the most sensitive correlation with human arboviral transmission risk, calculated as the total number of positive water containers harboring Aedes larvae or pupae per one hundred houses inspected. When the Breteau index exceeds twenty, the locality enters a high-risk transmission zone capable of explosive dengue transmission, prompting immediate civic sanitary interventions and thermal fogging.
steps.say: The Breteau index counts the number of positive water containers found per one hundred homes inspected. An index above twenty warns of an impending explosive dengue outbreak.

steps.title: House index and container index
steps.tx: Epidemiologists evaluate container distribution using the **House Index**, which denotes the percentage of inspected houses found positive for Aedes breeding, with values above five percent denoting transmission danger. Alongside this, the Container Index measures the percentage of all water-holding vessels positive for larvae; together, these three indices provide a comprehensive assessment of community container density and domestic water hygiene.
steps.say: The House Index measures the percentage of homes with mosquito breeding, while the Container Index measures the percentage of positive water vessels. A house index over five percent indicates danger.

steps.title: Chikungunya fever: clinical picture and epidemiology
steps.tx: Sharing identical Aedes mosquito vectors with dengue, the **chikungunya virus** is an alphavirus of the Togaviridae family that causes sudden high fever, debilitating symmetrical polyarthralgia, headaches and prominent maculopapular rash. Severe joint pain predominantly strikes peripheral small joints of the hands and feet, often leaving patients bedridden and hobbled, with disabling chronic inflammatory arthralgia persisting for months to years.
steps.say: Chikungunya causes high fever and severe, crippling joint pain that can linger for months or years. It is spread by the same Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue.

steps.title: Japanese encephalitis: vector and rural ecology
steps.tx: Unlike peri-domestic Aedes mosquitoes, the culicine species **Culex tritaeniorhynchus** serves as the principal vector of Japanese encephalitis across rural agrarian landscapes. This mosquito breeds abundantly in flooded paddy fields, shallow irrigation ditches, seepages and hyacinth-choked ponds; it displays twilight and nocturnal exophilic feeding habits, flying up to three kilometres between breeding rice fields and human settlements in search of blood.
steps.say: Culex tritaeniorhynchus breeds across flooded rice fields and ditches. It bites outdoors during evening twilight, carrying Japanese encephalitis virus across several kilometres.

steps.title: Animal hosts: amplifying vs dead-end hosts
steps.tx: In Japanese encephalitis transmission ecology, pigs and ardeid wading birds act as primary **amplifying hosts**, developing high-titre, prolonged viraemia without exhibiting clinical neurological disease, thereby infecting thousands of feeding Culex mosquitoes. In contrast, humans and domestic horses represent accidental dead-end hosts; the transient, low-titre viraemia produced during human infection is entirely insufficient to transmit the virus back to biting vectors.
steps.say: Pigs and wading birds multiply the virus to high concentrations without falling sick. Humans are dead-end hosts who develop encephalitis but cannot pass the virus back to mosquitoes.

steps.title: Japanese encephalitis clinical presentation
steps.tx: In endemic populations, the vast majority of Japanese encephalitis infections run an asymptomatic or mild febrile course, with only one in three hundred to one thousand infected individuals progressing to overt **acute encephalitis syndrome**. Those affected present with high fever, neck stiffness, stupor, convulsions, cogwheel rigidity and tremors due to basal ganglia necrosis, suffering a thirty percent fatality rate and lifelong neurological handicaps.
steps.say: Only one in several hundred infected patients develops overt brain inflammation. Those who do face a thirty percent mortality rate and frequent permanent neurological damage.

steps.title: Japanese encephalitis vaccination in endemic districts
steps.tx: Universal control in high-risk rural districts depends on the **Japanese encephalitis vaccine**, formulated as a live attenuated virus derived from the SA 14-14-2 strain and administered under the national immunization schedule. Children receive zero point five millilitres subcutaneously at nine completed months along with measles-rubella, followed by a second booster dose between sixteen and twenty-four months of age.
steps.say: Children in endemic districts receive the live attenuated SA 14-14-2 vaccine at nine months, followed by a booster dose in their second year to confer enduring immunity.

steps.title: Integrated vector management for arboviral control
steps.tx: Community-wide containment of arboviral fevers requires rigorous environmental **source reduction**, observing weekly dry days where all households completely drain, scrub and dry domestic water storage containers to disrupt the eight-day aquatic cycle. Non-potable water bodies receive temephos larvicide or diflubenzuron, while outdoor spaces undergo thermal fogging with pyrethrum during active epidemics to slash adult mosquito density.
steps.say: A weekly community dry day empties domestic containers to break the eight-day larval cycle. Temephos treats standing water, and thermal fogging knocks down adult mosquitoes during outbreaks.
